transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess what brings me in is… I feel like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. Like I’ll finish one thing at school or at home, and before I’ve even had a second to breathe, I’m already jumping into the next thing. It’s like I can’t shut myself off.

I’m a special education teacher, so there’s always something to do, of course, but this feels beyond just being busy. Even when the day is technically over, I’m still moving, still looking for the next task, the next thing to fix or start. It’s gotten to where I don’t really feel like I can just stop and be still. That’s the main reason I thought I should come talk to someone.
Do you find it difficult to focus on one task for an extended period of time?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean, I can focus when I need to, especially if something is right in front of me and it’s urgent or it involves one of my students. But “for an extended period of time”… I guess I’d have to think about what you mean by that.

I don’t know that I’ve noticed focus being the main issue, exactly. It’s more that I’m always kind of moving from thing to thing, but I’m not sure if that’s the same as not being able to focus. Like, if I have paperwork or planning or a meeting, I can usually get through it, though I might feel kind of restless while I’m doing it. But I wouldn’t want to say I can’t focus, because that doesn’t feel quite accurate.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Yes… I think that’s probably true, though I don’t always recognize it in the moment as “acting on impulse.” It’s more like I jump in before I’ve really thought about whether I should.

The biggest thing I notice is in conversations. At school, if colleagues are talking through a situation with a student, or if I’m in a conversation with a parent, I’ll suddenly cut in because I think I know where it’s going or I think I can help solve it faster. And I really do mean it as helping — I’m not trying to be rude — but then I realize I’ve talked over someone or kind of taken charge of the conversation before they even finished their thought.

It happens at home too. My spouse might be talking with a relative, and I’ll jump in with what I think is the answer or the next step, and then afterward I can tell I bulldozed the moment. It’s like my mouth gets there before the rest of me has a chance to decide if I should speak. I feel bad about it afterward, because I don’t want people to feel dismissed, but in the moment it feels urgent, like I need to say it right then.
Do you often find yourself talking more than others in social situations?

Yes. Yeah, I do. Probably more than I realize in the moment.

It shows up a lot at work. I’ll go into a parent conference or a staff meeting telling myself, okay, just answer the question, keep it short, don’t take over the room. And then somehow I hear myself giving three different examples, then a story from my classroom, then a couple of ideas nobody even asked me for. And while I’m talking, part of me can see the other person is trying to wrap things up — like they’re looking at the clock, or they’ve already kind of nodded enough times — but I keep going because I feel like I need to finish the whole thought.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I don’t mean to dominate the conversation. I usually think I’m being thorough or helpful, especially with parents or staff because I care about getting it right. But then afterward I replay it and think, why did I say all of that? They asked one question and I gave them a whole seminar.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're sitting still?

Yes. Very much so. Sitting still is actually one of the things people can see on me before I even notice I’m doing it.

In IEP meetings, for example, I’ll be at the table trying to listen and be professional, and my leg is just bouncing under the table the whole time. Or I’ll be clicking a pen, or shifting around in the chair, leaning forward, leaning back, crossing and uncrossing my legs. Sometimes I don’t even realize it until someone glances over at me, and then I’m like, oh, I’m doing it again.

It happens in my admin classes too. If I’m sitting for any length of time, I feel like there’s this pressure in my body to move somehow. I can keep myself in the chair, but it takes effort. I’ll tell myself, stop clicking the pen, stop moving your leg, just sit still, and then two minutes later I’m doing some other version of it. It’s embarrassing because I know it can be distracting to other people, but half the time it feels automatic.
Do you have difficulty managing your emotions, such as feeling overly angry or irritable?

I’m not really sure on that one. I mean, I get irritated like anyone does, especially when there’s a lot going on, but I don’t know that I’d describe myself as overly angry.

Sometimes I probably sound more intense than I mean to, and people might read that as irritation, but from inside it doesn’t always feel like anger. It’s more like I’m trying to get a point across or respond quickly, and then afterward I might think, okay, maybe that came out sharper than I intended. But I don’t know if that’s the same as having trouble managing emotions.

I wouldn’t say I’m someone who’s constantly blowing up or anything like that. At least I don’t think so. My family might have their own view, I guess, but from my perspective, anger isn’t the main thing I notice.
Do you ever feel extremely happy or euphoric for no apparent reason?

Not really, no. I mean, I can be in a good mood, obviously, and there are times I get excited about something going well — like if a lesson clicks or a student has a good day — but I wouldn’t describe it as extremely happy or euphoric out of nowhere.

If anything, my energy can be high sometimes, and maybe people might think I’m more animated than the situation calls for, but inside it doesn’t feel like some random wave of happiness. It’s usually tied to something. I don’t have those moments where I’m just suddenly on top of the world for no reason that I can identify. At least not that I’ve noticed.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings of restlessness and constantly being on the go?

I’d say this level of it has been going on for about eight months now. I mean, I’ve probably always been a person who moves around a lot, but the point where it really became harder to ignore — where I felt constantly on edge or like I couldn’t settle — was around eight months ago.

That was when our older relative moved in with us, and things at home changed quite a bit. Since then, it’s like the restlessness has been turned up. I’m sitting there and I just feel like I need to be doing something or moving somehow. So, yes, about eight months, give or take.
Have these feelings of restlessness and constantly being on the go caused any problems for you at work, at home, or in your relationships?

Yes. I mean… unfortunately, yes, it has caused problems. I think for a while I was trying to tell myself it was just stress or that I was just being productive, but it’s gotten to the point where other people are clearly affected by it.

At work, it’s become serious. I’m a special education teacher, and the pace and the interruptions are already a lot, but my restlessness and feeling like I have to jump in or move things along has led to complaints. It’s not just casual comments anymore — I was actually put on a corrective plan. That was hard to hear, because in my mind I’m trying to help, trying to respond quickly, trying to keep things from falling through the cracks. But I guess the way it comes across is disruptive or like I’m not trusting the process, or not giving colleagues enough room. And that’s been embarrassing, honestly.

At home it’s been a problem too. My spouse has said the caregiving routines are harder because people aren’t just dealing with the actual caregiving — they’re also having to manage my energy, if that makes sense. Like instead of me calming the situation or being steady, I can add this extra layer of intensity. I’m pacing, asking what’s next, trying to fix things, maybe pushing too fast. And I don’t mean to make it harder, but I can see how I do.

The part that bothers me most is I feel like I’m damaging trust. With colleagues, with my family. I want people to see that I’m trying to help, but I think sometimes they experience me as one more thing they have to manage. That’s… that’s not how I want to be.
Have you noticed any significant strain on your relationships with family or friends due to your constant need to be on the go and restless?

Yes, definitely. I mean, I don’t like admitting that, but yes. At home especially, my spouse has basically said that the routines around caregiving are already hard enough, and then on top of that people have to sort of manage my energy too. Like I’m moving around, asking what needs to happen next, trying to jump in and solve things, and I think I believe I’m helping in the moment, but I can see how it makes everything feel more tense.

And it’s not just home. With work, the complaints have gotten serious enough that I was put on a corrective plan, which was honestly upsetting and embarrassing. I think colleagues may feel like I’m pushing too much or not letting things unfold, even though my intention is to help and keep things moving.

So yes, I do feel like it’s putting strain on relationships. The thing that bothers me most is this feeling that I’m damaging trust with people — my family, my coworkers — because they don’t just see me as helpful. They see me as another thing they have to handle. And that’s really hard to sit with.
Have you had to make any significant adjustments to your daily routine or responsibilities due to these feelings of restlessness and constant need to be on the go?

Yes, I’ve had to adjust things, although I’m not sure I’ve adjusted them in a very organized way. It’s more like people around me and I have had to work around my energy, if that makes sense.

At work, it’s become serious enough that I can’t just say, “Oh, this is my style” or “I’m just trying to stay on top of things.” There have been enough complaints that I was put on a corrective plan, so now I have to be more careful about how I enter situations, how quickly I jump in, how much I push things along. I’m trying to pause more, but honestly it takes a lot of effort, and I don’t always get it right.

At home, the adjustments are more emotional and practical. My spouse has told me that caregiving routines are harder because it’s not just the caregiving itself — people are also having to manage my energy. Like if I’m pacing or asking what needs to happen next or trying to fix everything at once, then I become another thing everyone has to deal with. So I’ve had to try to step back more, or at least be aware that my version of “helping” can make things more tense.

And that’s probably the hardest part. I feel like I’m damaging trust with my colleagues and with my family, even though in my mind I’m trying to help. So the adjustments are partly to my responsibilities, but also to how I show up around people. I’m trying to not be so much… in the middle of everything all the time.
Have you had difficulty completing tasks or projects due to your restlessness and constant need to be on the go?

Yes… yes, I think so. It’s a little hard for me to explain, because I don’t always stop a task in the obvious way, like just abandoning it completely. It’s more that I’m constantly moving from one thing to the next before I’ve really fully finished or settled anything.

What brings me in, honestly, is that lately I feel like I’m running on a motor all the time. Like at school, I’ll finish one thing — or think I’ve finished it — and then immediately I’m onto the next thing, and then the next, and there’s no real pause where I can sort of close the loop. And the same thing happens at home. I can’t just finish something and sit with it or let it be done. My mind and body are already pushing me toward the next responsibility, the next problem, the next thing that needs attention.

So yes, it does make completing tasks harder, because even when I’m doing a lot, it doesn’t always feel complete or organized. It’s like I’m in motion constantly, but not necessarily landing the plane, if that makes sense. I keep thinking, “Okay, after this I’ll slow down,” but then I don’t. I just jump into whatever is next.
Have you experienced any significant difficulties in your personal relationships due to your behavior or symptoms?

Yes, I have. I wish I could say it was just stress or that people are misunderstanding me, but it’s become pretty clear that my behavior is affecting my relationships.

At work, it’s not just one awkward conversation here or there. The complaints got serious enough that I was put on a corrective plan, which was really hard to hear. I’m a teacher, and I care a lot about doing a good job and being dependable, so to have colleagues feel like my way of operating is causing problems… that really shook me. I think they experience me as too much sometimes, like I’m pushing into things or trying to manage everything, even when I honestly think I’m helping.

And at home, my spouse has been pretty direct with me that the caregiving routines are harder because people aren’t just dealing with the routines themselves — they’re also having to manage my energy. That was painful to hear, because in my mind I’m trying to be useful, trying to stay ahead of things, trying to make sure nothing falls apart. But I can see how it comes across differently, like I’m adding tension instead of reducing it.

So yes, personally and professionally, it’s caused real difficulty. The part that bothers me most is that I feel like I’m damaging trust with people. My family and coworkers may not see my intentions anymore — they just see the impact. And that’s a hard thing to sit with.
Have you felt like your symptoms are affecting your overall quality of life?

Yes, very much so. I don’t think it’s just an inconvenience anymore, or just me being “busy” or energetic. It’s affecting how safe and steady my life feels, if that makes sense.

At work, the complaints have become serious enough that I was put on a corrective plan, and that’s been really upsetting. I’m a special education teacher, and I care a lot about being reliable and supportive, so having my colleagues feel like my way of operating is causing problems has made me question myself all the time. I feel like I’m walking around trying to monitor everything I say and do, but even then I worry I’m still coming across as too much.

And at home, it’s affecting the atmosphere there too. My spouse has said caregiving routines are harder because people have to manage my energy on top of everything else. That one really hurts, because I think I’m helping — I’m trying to anticipate things, jump in, keep things moving — but instead it sounds like I’m becoming another burden in the room.

So yes, it’s definitely affecting my quality of life. I feel like I’m damaging trust with people I care about and people I work with, even though my intention is not to make things harder. It leaves me feeling embarrassed, tense, and honestly kind of sad, because I don’t want to be someone people have to brace themselves for.
Have you felt like you're unable to enjoy activities you used to due to these feelings of restlessness and constant need to be on the go?

Yes… I think that’s actually a big part of it. It’s not that I don’t want to enjoy things, or that the activities themselves have stopped mattering to me. It’s more like I can’t ever really settle into them anymore.

What brings me in is that lately I feel like I’m constantly running on a motor. I’ll finish one thing at school — or at least get it to a point where I think it’s finished — and then immediately I’m already jumping into the next thing. And then I do the same thing at home. There’s no real off switch. Even if I’m technically doing something I used to enjoy, part of me is already moving ahead to the next task or the next thing that needs to be handled.

So yes, it makes enjoyment harder, because I don’t feel present. I’m physically there, but internally I’m already pushing forward. I don’t really get that feeling of relaxing into something or feeling satisfied after finishing it. It’s like everything turns into one more stop on a conveyor belt, and I’m just trying to keep up with it.
Have you considered that your symptoms might be part of a larger pattern that is affecting multiple areas of your life?

Yes, I have, and I think that’s part of what’s been so hard to admit. For a while I kept treating each situation like it was separate — like, “Okay, this is a work problem,” or “This is just tension at home,” or “Maybe people are just stressed right now.” But when I step back, it does feel like the same pattern is showing up in more than one place.

At work, the complaints have gotten serious enough that I was put on a corrective plan, and that was kind of a wake-up call. I’m not just occasionally rubbing someone the wrong way — it’s affecting how people experience working with me. And at home, my spouse has said that caregiving routines are harder because it’s not only the routine itself people are managing, they’re also managing my energy on top of everything else.

That’s the part that really bothers me, because in my head I’m trying to help. I’m trying to be useful, to stay on top of things, to make sure things don’t fall through the cracks. But the impact seems to be that people feel worn out by me or like they can’t fully trust how I’m going to show up. I feel like I’m damaging trust with colleagues and with my family, even though that’s the opposite of what I want.

So yes… I do think it’s a larger pattern. It’s not contained in one area anymore. It’s following me from work to home, and it’s affecting the people I care about and the people I depend on professionally.
Do you feel like your symptoms are interfering with your ability to perform daily tasks or maintain a regular routine?

Yes, definitely. I mean, I wish I could say it was just an occasional thing, but it’s interfering with daily routines in a way that other people are noticing and reacting to now.

At work, it’s gotten serious enough that the complaints about how I operate led to me being put on a corrective plan. That’s not just a small misunderstanding anymore. I’m a special education teacher, so my day depends on consistency, communication, and being someone people can rely on. And when colleagues are saying my way of doing things is creating problems, it makes me feel like I’m not maintaining the professional routine I need to maintain, even though I’m trying very hard to stay on top of everything.

At home it shows up too. My spouse has told me that caregiving routines are harder because everyone is managing my energy on top of the actual tasks. That was hard to hear, because in my mind I’m helping — I’m jumping in, trying to keep things moving, trying to anticipate what needs to happen next. But apparently the way I do that can make the routine feel more chaotic or exhausting for everyone else.

So yes, it interferes with daily tasks and keeping a regular routine. The hardest part is that I feel like I’m damaging trust with both my colleagues and my family, even though my intention is to be helpful and dependable. Instead, I think people feel like they have to brace themselves for me, and that’s really upsetting.
Have you noticed your relationships with others changing as a result of your constant restlessness and need to be on the go?

Yes. I think that’s one of the biggest changes I’ve noticed, honestly. It’s not just that I feel restless inside — it’s that other people seem to have to adjust themselves around it.

At work, it’s gotten to the point where the complaints were serious enough that I was put on a corrective plan, and that was really hard to take in. I don’t think I realized how much my way of moving through the day was affecting people until it became formal like that. I thought I was being proactive or trying to keep things moving, but I think colleagues may experience me as exhausting, or hard to work with, or maybe not as steady as they need me to be.

And at home, my spouse has said something similar in a different way — that caregiving routines are harder because people aren’t just managing the tasks, they’re also managing my energy. That hurt to hear, but I also can’t say it’s completely wrong. I can come in trying to help, trying to anticipate the next thing, trying to speed things along, but the effect can be that everyone else feels more tense or overwhelmed.

So yes, my relationships feel different. I feel like I’m damaging trust with both my colleagues and my family, even though I’m honestly trying to help. That’s the part I keep getting stuck on — my intention is to be useful and reliable, but the impact seems to be that people brace themselves around me.

Do you think your restlessness and constant need to be on the go are more related to having trouble sitting still and being patient, or to having trouble focusing on one task and seeing it through to completion?

I think it’s more the sitting still and being patient part. I mean, I can get pulled off course too, but when you ask it that way, the thing people actually see is that I just don’t stay seated when I’m supposed to.

Like if I’m in a training at school, I’ll tell myself I’m going to sit there and be respectful and just get through it, but then I start feeling like I need to do something. So I’ll find a reason — I need more water, I should check whether the copier is free, I forgot to look at something in the hallway. Sometimes it’s not even that important, but in the moment it feels like I have to get up.

Same thing at dinner with my family. I know I should just sit and be present, but I’m up getting something, checking on something, moving around the kitchen, looking in on my relative. And in school meetings, I’ll have this urge to step out or “just quickly” check on something, even when I know it probably looks rude or disrespectful.

That’s what bothers me, because I’m not trying to send the message that I don’t care. I do care. I’m usually very aware afterward that it may have come across badly. But in the moment, sitting there and waiting feels almost impossible, like my body is looking for an excuse to move before I’ve even fully decided to.
Do you think your mind wanders or you get distracted more often than you feel the physical need to move or fidget?

I do get distracted, but honestly the physical part is more obvious to me — or maybe more obvious to other people before I even catch it.

Like in IEP meetings or in my admin classes, I’ll realize my leg has been bouncing under the table the whole time. Or I’m clicking a pen, shifting around in the chair, changing position over and over. Sometimes I don’t even notice I’m doing it until someone glances over, and then I suddenly become aware of it and feel embarrassed, like, “Oh, I’m doing that again.”

It’s not always that my mind has wandered off somewhere else first. Sometimes I’m still listening, or at least trying to listen, but my body is just… going. My leg is moving, my hands need something to do, I’m fidgeting in the chair. And then once I notice people noticing it, I get self-conscious, which makes it harder to just sit normally.

So if I had to choose, I’d say the need to move or fidget is more noticeable than my mind wandering. At least that’s the part that seems to show up in a way other people can see.

In IEP meetings, for example, I’ll be at the table trying to listen and be professional, and my leg is just bouncing under the table the whole time. doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, or a combination of both
doctor.question: Do you think your restlessness and constant need to be on the go are more related to having trouble sitting still and being patient, or to having trouble focusing on one task and seeing it through to completion?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: When I’m supposed to sit through a training, dinner with the family, or a school meeting, I keep finding reasons to get up—refill water, check the copier, look in on my relative—even when I know it makes me look disrespectful.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the restlessness is more about trouble sitting still and being patient versus task focus; the symptom profile most directly related to trouble sitting still is leaving the seat when remaining seated is expected.

patient.answer:
I think it’s more the sitting still and being patient part. I mean, I can get pulled off course too, but when you ask it that way, the thing people actually see is that I just don’t stay seated when I’m supposed to.

Like if I’m in a training at school, I’ll tell myself I’m going to sit there and be respectful and just get through it, but then I start feeling like I need to do something. So I’ll find a reason — I need more water, I should check whether the copier is free, I forgot to look at something in the hallway. Sometimes it’s not even that important, but in the moment it feels like I have to get up.

Same thing at dinner with my family. I know I should just sit and be present, but I’m up getting something, checking on something, moving around the kitchen, looking in on my relative. And in school meetings, I’ll have this urge to step out or “just quickly” check on something, even when I know it probably looks rude or disrespectful.

That’s what bothers me, because I’m not trying to send the message that I don’t care. I do care. I’m usually very aware afterward that it may have come across badly. But in the moment, sitting there and waiting feels almost impossible, like my body is looking for an excuse to move before I’ve even fully decided to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily driven by inattention or hyperactivity
doctor.question: Do you think your mind wanders or you get distracted more often than you feel the physical need to move or fidget?

target_item.name: Fidgeting

patient.answer:
I do get distracted, but honestly the physical part is more obvious to me — or maybe more obvious to other people before I even catch it.

Like in IEP meetings or in my admin classes, I’ll realize my leg has been bouncing under the table the whole time. Or I’m clicking a pen, shifting around in the chair, changing position over and over. Sometimes I don’t even notice I’m doing it until someone glances over, and then I suddenly become aware of it and feel embarrassed, like, “Oh, I’m doing that again.”

It’s not always that my mind has wandered off somewhere else first. Sometimes I’m still listening, or at least trying to listen, but my body is just… going. My leg is moving, my hands need something to do, I’m fidgeting in the chair. And then once I notice people noticing it, I get self-conscious, which makes it harder to just sit normally.

So if I had to choose, I’d say the need to move or fidget is more noticeable than my mind wandering. At least that’s the part that seems to show up in a way other people can see.
